title: What to say
hook: a blank text box after a death, and five marks of well-spoken words
tomorrow: why would anyone chant to someone too sick to answer?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a basin of water before any words: just be there. Today closes the week on grief, with the question that comes next.

A friend's message says someone they love has died. The reply box sits there, blinking. People type and delete. Some send a heart and nothing else, then worry about it for a week. Everything sounds wrong: too much, too little, too much like a card. So when you do have to speak, what do you say? The suttas have a short list for exactly this kind of moment, though it was never written only for funerals.
screen: `THE REPLY BOX BLINKS.` → `TYPE, DELETE, TYPE.` → `WHAT DO YOU SAY?`

segments.voice: In one sutta the Buddha names five marks of well-spoken words. They're spoken at the right time. They're true. They're gentle. They're helpful. And they're spoken with a mind of goodwill. Notice what isn't on the list: clever, complete, or long. In another sutta, the Buddha says of his own speech that he says only what is true and helpful, and he waits for the right time to say even a hard thing. So the words that fit a loss tend to be small. Not: at least she isn't suffering. Not: I know exactly how you feel. Those can sound wise and still land wrong. I'm so sorry. I'm here. I loved her laugh. True, gentle, on time. And timing matters: a true thing said too soon can still land hard. Silence is allowed too, the kind that stays in the room. That's the week, and it holds together. A mother walked a whole street and found no house untouched. A queen's questions showed that grief is love. Even Ananda wept, and his teacher sent for him. A warm mug showed that grief can be held gently. A gift given in someone's name is for them. And a basin of water said: just be there. Today adds the smallest piece. When words are needed, simple words.
screen: `FIVE MARKS OF WELL-SPOKEN WORDS.` · `NOT CLEVER, NOT LONG.` · `SILENCE IS ALLOWED.` · `A WEEK OF GRIEF, HELD.` · then, large: `SIMPLE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who's carrying something heavy right now. In your head or on your phone, shape one short sentence for them that is true, gentle and kind, and nothing more. Read it back slowly, and take out any word that's trying too hard, any advice, any silver lining; what's left is usually enough. Keep it ready to send when the time is right.
What to say: words at the right time, true, gentle, helpful and kind, from a mind of goodwill. Small is fine. Silence that stays in the room is fine too.
Keep this: simple words, because I'm sorry, I'm here, is a whole sentence. Twenty days of thirty, and a week of grief, walked through.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice right speech as part of the eightfold path; at a death, condolences in Buddhist communities are often brief, with a bow, joined palms or a few quiet words to the family.

match.prompt: the five marks of well-spoken words — tap the pairs.

myth: the best condolence is a long, wise message
the five marks are timely, true, gentle, helpful and kind. long and clever aren't on the list.
the sutta's marks of good speech include being spoken at the right time
timing is the first of the five.
saying nothing at all is always a failure of kindness
a silence that stays in the room can be the kindest thing on hand.

fork.setup: at the funeral, your friend's aunt asks you how her nephew is doing. honestly, he's a mess. what fits the five marks?
options: tell her he's doing great, so she won't worry today.
say gently that he's hurting, and that you're staying close to him.
list everything that's gone wrong for him this month, so she knows.
fork.reveal: true and gentle, at the right time, with goodwill. no comforting lie, no flood of detail.

original.note: Pali samma vaca: right speech, a step of the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: comfort means finding the perfect thing to say.
what it means: words that are timely, true, gentle, helpful and kind, and they can be very few. silence counts.
what a scholar hears: Anguttara Nikaya 5.198 lists the five factors of well-spoken speech; Majjhima Nikaya 58 adds that the Buddha weighed truth, benefit and timing before speaking.
guess: a few true, gentle words at the right time, or a kind silence
a set prayer every Buddhist must recite at a funeral
a polite way to change the subject away from the death

chat.says: ava's grandma died last night. i'm walking over to her house now. what do i even say
options: something small and true: i'm so sorry, i'm here. then let the quiet do the rest.
remind her everything happens for a reason, and she'll feel better soon.
tell her what helped you when you lost someone, so she has a plan.
chat.meaning: Well-spoken words are timely, true, gentle, helpful and kind. A few simple words and a kind silence fit a loss.

tie.story: The Buddha named five marks of well-spoken words: timely, true, gentle, helpful, and spoken with goodwill.
tie.friend: Mai can walk in with a few simple words for Ava, and let staying close say the rest.
tie.you: who needs a short, true sentence from you?

suttas.meaning: discourses of the Buddha, in the Pali texts

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's cousin and longtime attendant

goodwill.meaning: a kind wish for the other's good; in Pali, metta

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.198, Vaca Sutta (five factors of well-spoken speech: timely, true, gentle, beneficial, with a mind of goodwill)
Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the Buddha speaks what is true and beneficial, knowing the right time)
